I have just received a new laptop and I want to make an image of the entire hard disk before I install linux on it. Ideally I want the software to understand the NTFS partition and not copy the empty space on it. I would also want it to copy the Windows boot loader/partition too.
I'd suggest gparted and cpio. Might not be as user friendly as you'd like it, but more than dd.
since you got some answers may I ask why you don't like using dd? it's always made perfect 1:1 copies for me.
Doesn't dd copy the empty space also?

Arch has a great suggestion for that. Pipe dd into gzip.

dd if=/dev/sdX conv=sync,noerror bs=64K | gzip -c > /path/to/backup.img.gz

To get the image back:

gunzip -c /path/to/backup.img.gz | dd of=/dev/sdX

Or if you split the image across multiple files:

cat /path/to/backup.img.gz* | gunzip -c | dd of=/dev/sdX

Note: I haven't had success with the multiple file one, but I'm probably doing something wrong.

https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/disk_cloning

If you want to access the files on the image without reimaging it to a physical disk (as long as you didn't split the image across multiple files), you can do this and mount it as a loop device temporarily:

https://major.io/2010/12/14/mounting-a-raw-partition-file-made-with-dd-or-dd_rescue-in-linux/

I recommend imaging the disk by partition, just so you have separate image files by partition when handling it. Depending on what's on the disk (like a Windows install for example), this can make handling/reimaging easier. Just depends though.

I have done a similar thing in the past, except with lzop, which provides dramatically more speed but somewhat less compresssion.
